headline: Self-driving toilet navigates homes, cleans itself, and empties waste
summary: The autonomous Xiaoban toilet uses lidar and ultrasonic sensors to navigate homes, and features a bidet, warm air dryer, and self-cleaning bowl. It aims to improve accessibility for those with mobility issues.
details: A Chinese company called Yueban has debuted the Xiaoban, a smart toilet designed to improve accessibility for individuals with mobility challenges. This autonomous, self-driving toilet can navigate homes, clean itself, and empty its waste, offering greater independence to users.

Utilizing technology similar to advanced robot vacuums, the Xiaoban employs lidar and ultrasonic sensors to autonomously plan safe routes. It can be summoned via remote or voice commands, allowing users to remain in their rooms without needing to relocate to a bathroom.

The toilet is equipped with a built-in bidet and a warm air drying mechanism for cleaning. It also features a self-cleaning bowl system that seals waste in an enclosed receptacle, along with UV lights to kill bacteria and minimize odors.

After use, the Xiaoban can either recharge and empty its pulverized waste into a connected dock with plumbing, or if no drainage is available, it will pump the waste into a traditional toilet via an extending arm.

While not a complete replacement for caregivers, the Xiaoban significantly eases their burden by handling waste disposal and reducing the need for assistance in moving to a bathroom. It is expected to sell for approximately $4,300 in China, with global availability yet to be confirmed.

topic: apple opens third-party app stores in brazil
headline_marked: Apple allows [[third-party app stores in Brazil]] with 5% fee
headline: Apple allows third-party app stores in Brazil with 5% fee
summary: Apple opens up App Store to new competition in Brazil, with a 5% Core Technology Fee for apps distributed outside the App Store.
details: Apple is beginning to allow alternative app stores for iOS customers in Brazil. The company had reached an agreement with the Conselho Administrativo de Defesa Econômica (CADE), the Brazilian government's competition regulator, around how the third-party marketplaces would work domestically.

The Core Technology Fee for apps distributed outside the App Store will be 5 percent. Any alternatives to the App Store will have to be approved by Apple, and apps sold through them will face a review process called Notarization.

This review will be less comprehensive than the usual App Store review while still ideally catching instances of malware, viruses or other security threats. The plan for Brazil, including the Notarization review, is similar to how the company has handled third-party marketplaces across Europe as that region began enforcing the Digital Markets Act.
